question: Best fractional CRO for a Series B company?
body:
## Direct Answer

The best fractional CRO for a Series B company is a former VP or CRO who has personally scaled a comparable business from roughly two to ten million or ten to thirty million in ARR, works two to three days a week, and installs a repeatable revenue system rather than just selling. Prioritize pattern-match over pedigree: same motion, same buyer, same stage of scaling pain. There is no single "best" name — the right fractional CRO is the one whose last two operating chapters mirror the exact bottleneck your board is worried about right now.

Series B is the stage where a company has proven it can sell but has not yet proven it can scale selling. You have product-market fit, a handful of reps who close, and a board that just wrote a large check expecting the revenue line to bend upward predictably. A fractional Chief Revenue Officer is a senior operator who owns that "make it predictable" problem part-time — typically two to three days a week over a six-to-twelve-month engagement — for a fraction of the cost and dilution of a full-time hire. The question is not whether to consider one, but how to pick the one whose scars match your specific scaling wall. The rest of this guide is a field manual for that decision: what the role actually owns at your stage, how to grade pattern-match, where to source real operators, how to structure comp and exit so the incentives point at *your* outcome, and the failure modes that quietly waste six months and a board's patience.

## What does a Series B company actually need from a fractional CRO?

At Series B, the failure mode is rarely "we can't sell." It is "we can't sell *repeatably*, and we don't know which of our numbers to trust." Founders and early sales leaders got the company here on hustle, warm intros, and heroic individual deals. That engine does not survive contact with a hiring plan that doubles headcount in twelve months. The fractional CRO's job is to convert founder-led, hero-led revenue into a *system* — defined stages, honest forecasting, a repeatable ramp for new reps, and a go-to-market motion that a board can model.

Concretely, that means a Series B fractional CRO should own four things in their first two quarters: diagnosing the true state of pipeline and forecast accuracy; defining or rebuilding the sales process and stage definitions so the CRM tells the truth; standing up onboarding and enablement so rep number eight ramps as fast as rep number three; and building the operating cadence — the weekly forecast call, the monthly business review, the quarterly board narrative — that keeps everyone honest. Notice how little of that is "personally close deals." A fractional CRO who spends their two days a week carrying a bag is a very expensive senior rep, not a leader. The ones worth hiring build the machine and then hand you the keys. For the underlying discipline, see our primer on [building a repeatable revenue engine](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11133).

It helps to be specific about why Series B is the exact moment this role earns its keep. At seed and Series A, the founder is usually still the best salesperson in the building, and rightly so — nobody else can articulate the vision or improvise around an unfinished product the way the person who invented it can. That founder-led motion is a feature, not a bug, until roughly the point where the deal volume outgrows the number of hours the founder can personally spend in front of buyers. Series B capital is priced on the assumption that the company will now *break that dependency* and turn selling into something a team of hired reps can execute without the founder in every room. The fractional CRO exists precisely to manage that transition. They are not there to replace the founder's selling instinct; they are there to extract it, document it, and make it teachable so it survives the founder stepping back.

There is also a diagnostic dimension that founders routinely under-appreciate. Before anyone can fix a Series B revenue engine, someone senior has to establish what is actually true — and at this stage the numbers are almost always dirtier than leadership believes. Pipeline is inflated with stale deals nobody has the heart to close-lost. Stage definitions are subjective, so "50 percent to close" means something different for every rep. Forecast calls are optimism theater rather than commitment discipline. A strong fractional CRO spends their first weeks less as a builder and more as an auditor, separating the revenue the company can genuinely rely on from the revenue it merely hopes for. That honest baseline is often the single most valuable deliverable of the entire engagement, because every downstream decision — the hiring plan, the board narrative, the burn — depends on it being real.

## How do I evaluate a fractional CRO's pattern-match to my stage?

Pattern-match is the single highest-signal filter, and most founders under-weight it because they get dazzled by a big logo on a resume. A CRO who ran a two-thousand-person sales org at a public company has almost nothing useful to say about your eight-person team fighting for its first repeatable playbook — those are different jobs that happen to share a title. What you want is someone whose *most recent operating chapters* look like the movie you are about to live: scaling from single-digit to low-double-digit millions in ARR, in a comparable go-to-market motion, selling to a comparable buyer.

Break "pattern-match" into four concrete dimensions and grade each candidate honestly. First, **motion**: product-led, sales-led, or hybrid — a PLG expert can be actively wrong for a six-figure enterprise deal cycle. Second, **buyer and deal size**: selling a fifty-dollar-a-month SMB tool is a volume-and-velocity game; selling a two-hundred-thousand-dollar enterprise platform is a complex-sale game, and the playbooks barely overlap. Third, **stage of scaling pain**: zero-to-one product-market-fit hunting is a different sport from one-to-ten repeatability, which is different again from ten-to-fifty efficiency. Fourth, **outcome, not title**: what specifically did they change, and what moved as a result? Push every candidate to walk you through one engagement in forensic detail — what they inherited, the three changes they made, and the metric each change moved.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Series B revenue problem] --> B{What is the true bottleneck}
  B --> C[Forecast is unreliable]
  B --> D[Reps do not ramp]
  B --> E[Motion does not repeat]
  C --> F[Hire operator who fixed forecasting]
  D --> G[Hire operator who built enablement]
  E --> H[Hire operator who built playbook]
  F --> I[Verify with reference calls]
  G --> I
  H --> I
  I --> J[Scoped engagement with clear exit]
```

The diagram above captures the core move: name the bottleneck first, then match the operator to *that* bottleneck rather than to a generic "revenue leader" archetype. A founder who skips the diagnosis and hires on charisma tends to get a charismatic person who solves a problem the company did not actually have.

The forensic-detail interview is where pattern-match either holds up or falls apart, so it is worth scripting deliberately rather than winging. Ask a candidate to pick the single engagement most similar to your situation and then refuse to let them stay abstract. When they inherited the team, what was the ramp time for a new rep, and what was it when they left? What was forecast accuracy at the start, and how did they measure it? Which two or three deals did they lose that taught them something about the motion? Operators who genuinely did the work answer these instantly and specifically, often with numbers and named tradeoffs, because they lived the details. People who supervised from a height or who are inflating a thinner résumé retreat into frameworks and adjectives — "I drove alignment," "I built a high-performance culture" — because they never actually held the granular reality you are asking about. The specificity of the answer *is* the signal.

One useful mental model: you are not hiring for the average of a career, you are hiring for the relevance of its last chapter or two. A revenue leader who spent fifteen years at enterprise giants and the last three at a Series B startup that looked like yours is a strong match; the same leader minus that recent startup chapter is a risk, because the muscle memory that matters most — building with almost no infrastructure, doing the spreadsheet yourself, coaching a green rep — atrophies fast in a big-company environment. Weight recency heavily, and be honest with yourself when a shiny résumé is impressive in ways that are irrelevant to the specific problem in front of you.

## Where do I actually find qualified fractional CROs?

There are four channels, and they trade off differently on trust, speed, and cost. The highest-trust channel is your **investor and board network**. Your Series B lead has a portfolio full of companies at your exact stage and often maintains a bench of fractional and interim operators they have seen deliver. A warm introduction from a partner who has watched someone perform is worth more than any marketplace profile, because the reference is already baked in. Ask your board directly: "Who is the best part-time revenue leader you have seen work in a portfolio company like ours?"

The second channel is **operator communities and peer networks** — groups like Pavilion, which is built specifically for revenue leaders, plus founder Slack and peer CEO groups where recommendations carry accountability. The third is **fractional-executive marketplaces and firms** that vet and match part-time leaders; these move faster and offer more structure but require you to do your own diligence on fit. The fourth, and lowest-trust by default, is **inbound and self-promotion** — LinkedIn, cold outreach, content. Great operators exist here, but so does the largest volume of people who rebranded as "fractional CRO" the week after a layoff. Whatever the channel, the diligence bar does not move: you are hiring for a specific, verified operating outcome, not a title. Our guide to [structuring the search and interview loop](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/aq1158) walks through the sourcing sequence in more depth.

One caution worth stating plainly: "fractional CRO" is an unregulated label, and Series B is exactly the stage where the market fills with people whose experience is thinner than their deck. A genuine fractional CRO has *carried the quota and owned the number* as a full-time revenue leader before going part-time. Someone who was a sales manager or a solo consultant and adopted the title is not the same hire. Verify the operating history, not the branding.

A practical sourcing sequence keeps this from turning into an open-ended casting call that eats a quarter. Start narrow and warm: ask your two or three most credible investors and one or two founder peers each for a single name they would personally vouch for, and prioritize any name that surfaces from more than one source — convergence is a strong signal. Run those warm intros first, because they carry a pre-baked reference and close fastest. Only widen to communities and marketplaces if the warm well runs dry or the matches are off-stage. Treat inbound and self-promotion as a supplement, not a foundation; a great operator who found *you* is real, but you should still put them through the identical diligence you would apply to a marketplace stranger. Aim to run a genuine comparison of at least three credible candidates rather than falling in love with the first one who interviews well, both to calibrate your own sense of the market and to give yourself real leverage on scope and terms.

It is also worth being clear-eyed about what each channel actually costs you. The investor network is cheapest in dollars and highest in trust, but it can be narrow and occasionally conflicted — a partner may be steering you toward someone they want to keep busy, so still verify independently. Marketplaces and fractional firms cost more and add a matching fee or margin, but they compress the search timeline and often pre-vet operating history, which is worth real money when your board is impatient for a plan. The right answer for most Series B companies is a blend: mine the warm network first for trust, use a marketplace as a fast second source for breadth, and let the two candidate pools compete.

## How should I structure the engagement, comp, and exit?

Structure protects both sides and is where most fractional engagements quietly succeed or fail. Start with **time commitment**: two to three days a week is the realistic Series B band. Less than that and the CRO cannot hold the operating cadence; substantially more and you are drifting toward a full-time hire, which raises the fair question of whether you should just hire full-time. Set a **defined term** — a common shape is a three-month diagnostic-and-stabilize phase followed by a six-to-nine-month build phase, with an explicit checkpoint between them so either party can walk if the fit is wrong.

On **compensation**, expect a monthly retainer that reflects senior-operator seniority, often paired with meaningful equity because a fractional CRO shaping your revenue engine is closer to a founder-adjacent role than to a vendor. Avoid loading the package with pure closed-won commission — that incentivizes the CRO to become a rep and hoard deals instead of building the team's capacity. Tie a portion of variable comp to *system* outcomes you actually care about: forecast accuracy, new-rep ramp time, pipeline coverage discipline, the existence of a documented and adopted playbook. Most important, define the **exit and succession up front.** A fractional CRO is by design temporary; the engagement is a success when it makes itself unnecessary. Agree at the start on what "done" looks like — usually a hired full-time VP of Sales or CRO the fractional leader helped recruit and onboard, plus a revenue system that runs without them.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Month 0 to 3 Diagnose and stabilize] --> B[Month 3 checkpoint]
  B --> C[Month 3 to 9 Build the system]
  C --> D[Month 9 to 12 Recruit full time leader]
  D --> E[Handoff and exit]
  E --> F[System runs without the fractional CRO]
```

This phased shape keeps the relationship honest. The month-three checkpoint is a real off-ramp, not a formality — if the diagnosis reveals the two of you disagree on the core problem, that is the cheapest possible moment to part ways. And the built-in exit prevents the most common failure of a good engagement: a fractional CRO who quietly becomes permanent, blocking the full-time hire the company actually needs at Series C. For the operating-cadence templates, see our [revenue operating system reference](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11133).

A few structural details separate a clean engagement from a messy one. Put the scope in writing, and make it about deliverables rather than hours — "a documented sales process with stage exit criteria, a new-rep onboarding plan, and a functioning weekly forecast cadence by end of quarter two" is enforceable in a way that "three days a week of revenue leadership" is not. Agree explicitly on authority: does the fractional CRO manage the reps directly, or coach through the founder? Ambiguity here breeds resentment fast, because the team does not know whose direction to follow. Nail down decision rights on hiring — a fractional CRO who is accountable for the number but cannot influence who joins the team is set up to fail. And treat the equity conversation as a real one: vesting that aligns with the engagement's length and outcomes keeps the operator invested in a durable system rather than a quick surface polish, and it signals that you view them as a builder of lasting value rather than a temporary contractor to be squeezed on rate.

Finally, design the handoff, not just the hire. The most valuable output of a great fractional engagement is often the full-time successor the fractional leader recruits and trains — someone who inherits a working machine instead of a mess. Make that succession an explicit deliverable with its own timeline, and involve the fractional CRO in defining the full-time role's scorecard, interviewing candidates, and onboarding the winner. A fractional operator who is genuinely optimizing for your company's trajectory embraces this; one who dodges or delays it is quietly optimizing for their own tenure, which is a signal you will want to read carefully in the next section.

## What are the red flags and the failure modes?

The biggest red flag is the **quota-carrier in disguise** — the "fractional CRO" who, when you ask what they would do in the first ninety days, describes personally running deals. That person will drain their two days a week into a pipeline they own and leave you with the same non-scalable, hero-led revenue you started with, just more expensive. A leader builds capacity; a rep consumes it. Listen for whether their answers are about *the team's* output or *their own*.

The second failure mode is **stage mismatch masquerading as prestige** — the big-company executive who cannot function without a large team, a budget, and infrastructure they no longer have. At Series B, the CRO often has to build the spreadsheet themselves. Someone who has been ten years removed from hands-on work will stall. Third is **spreading too thin**: a fractional operator juggling five or six clients cannot give any one of them real attention. Ask directly how many concurrent engagements they carry; two or three is workable, six is a warning. Fourth is the **culture and buy-in gap** — a fractional CRO who parachutes in with a rigid playbook from their last company and refuses to adapt to your buyer and your team will generate resistance, not results. Finally, watch for **no clean exit plan.** If a candidate cannot articulate what "done" looks like or actively resists the idea of hiring their own full-time replacement, they may be optimizing for their own longevity over your company's trajectory. Diligence on all of these lives or dies on **reference calls** — talk to two or three founders who actually worked with this person, and ask what got worse as well as what got better.

Reference calls deserve more discipline than founders usually give them, because a bad hire here costs a full quarter of momentum you cannot get back. Insist on talking to a founder or CEO the candidate reported to, not just a friendly peer they hand-picked, and ideally reach one reference the candidate did *not* offer — a backdoor reference sourced through your own network tends to be far more candid. Ask outcome-anchored questions: what specifically did this person change, what number moved, and what would you have done differently about the engagement. Then ask the question most founders skip out of politeness — what got worse, what did they struggle with, and would you hire them again for the *exact* stage you are at now. The gap between an enthusiastic "yes, immediately" and a hedged "well, for the right situation" is where the truth lives.

There is one meta-failure worth naming above all the specific ones: hiring a fractional CRO to avoid making a decision you already need to make. Sometimes a founder reaches for a fractional leader because the real problem is that they have not decided what the go-to-market motion should be, or they are avoiding firing an underperforming early sales leader, or they simply want someone senior to blame if the number misses. A fractional CRO can diagnose and build, but they cannot substitute for founder conviction about the core strategy, and they cannot rescue a company that will not act on hard people decisions. Be honest with yourself about whether you are hiring an operator to solve a solvable execution problem — the good use of this role — or to postpone a leadership decision only you can make.

## Related questions

### How much does a fractional CRO cost at Series B?
Compensation is typically a senior-operator monthly retainer scaled to a two-to-three-day-a-week commitment, usually paired with meaningful equity. Exact figures vary widely by market, motion, and scope, so benchmark against several candidates rather than a single quoted rate, and avoid heavy closed-won commission that turns the leader into a rep.

### Fractional CRO vs. full-time VP of Sales — which first?
A fractional CRO is often the better first move at Series B because it buys senior strategic leadership and a diagnosis before you commit to an expensive full-time hire. A frequent pattern is a fractional CRO who builds the system *and* recruits the full-time VP or CRO who inherits it.

### How long should a fractional CRO engagement last?
Most run six to twelve months: a short diagnose-and-stabilize phase, a longer build phase, and a handoff. The engagement should be designed to end when a repeatable revenue system and a full-time successor are in place — a fractional CRO who never leaves is a warning sign.

### Can one fractional CRO fix both sales and marketing alignment?
Often yes, since "revenue" spans the full funnel and a strong CRO owns the sales-to-marketing handoff. But confirm the candidate's actual demand-generation experience — many revenue leaders are deep on sales and thin on marketing, so validate the half you most need.

### Is a fractional CRO worth it for a founder-led sales team?
Frequently yes, because founder-led sales is exactly the engine that stops scaling at Series B. A fractional CRO's core value is converting founder heroics into a documented, teachable system that survives the founder stepping back from every deal.

## FAQ

**What is a fractional CRO?**
A fractional Chief Revenue Officer is a senior revenue leader who works part-time — typically two to three days a week — owning a company's go-to-market strategy, sales process, forecasting, and team-building without the cost, equity, or permanence of a full-time executive hire.

**When is a company ready for a fractional CRO?**
Usually when it has clear product-market fit and early revenue but cannot yet make that revenue predictable or scale the team — which maps almost exactly onto the Series B stage. Before product-market fit, founders should still own selling directly.

**How is a fractional CRO different from a sales consultant?**
A consultant advises and hands you a deck; a fractional CRO takes operating ownership of the revenue number, runs the cadence, manages or coaches the team, and is accountable for outcomes. The difference is advice versus accountability.

**Should the fractional CRO carry a quota?**
Generally no. Their job is to build a team and system that hits the number, not to personally close deals. A fractional CRO who behaves like a senior rep is a red flag; tie their incentives to system outcomes like forecast accuracy and rep ramp instead.

**How many clients does a good fractional CRO take on?**
Two or three concurrent engagements is a workable ceiling for real attention. Six or more is a warning sign that no single client — including you — will get the focus a Series B scaling problem demands. Ask directly during diligence.

**What outcomes should I expect in the first ninety days?**
An honest diagnosis of pipeline and forecast health, redefined sales stages so the CRM tells the truth, the start of a repeatable onboarding motion, and an installed operating cadence — the weekly forecast call, monthly business review, and board-ready narrative. Deep team rebuilds come later.

**How do I know if a fractional CRO engagement is failing?**
Watch for the leader hoarding deals instead of building the team, refusing to adapt their playbook to your buyer, dodging reference-checkable outcomes, or resisting any conversation about their own exit and succession. Any of these signals that the engagement is drifting off its purpose.

**What is the ideal exit for a fractional CRO?**
A hired and onboarded full-time VP of Sales or CRO — often recruited with the fractional leader's help — inheriting a documented, adopted revenue system that runs without the fractional CRO present. Success is making the role unnecessary.

**Can a fractional CRO also help hire my full-time revenue leader?**
Yes, and the best ones treat it as a core deliverable rather than a favor. Because they have lived your motion and know exactly what the role requires, they can write the scorecard, screen candidates, and onboard the winner — turning their own exit into a clean handoff instead of a cliff.

**How is a fractional CRO different from an interim CRO?**
An interim CRO is a full-time placeholder covering a gap until a permanent hire lands; a fractional CRO is deliberately part-time and system-focused, designed to install repeatable revenue infrastructure a couple of days a week rather than to hold a seat until it can be filled.
